document.title: Motion to Intervene and Protest of the Retail Energy Supply Association re PJM Interconnection, LLC's proposed revisions to the Open Access Transmission Tariff

pages.text:
4900-3540-9097.1 
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA 
BEFORE THE 
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION 
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.  
) 
 Docket No. ER26-3380-000 
MOTION TO INTERVENE AND PROTEST OF 
THE RETAIL ENERGY SUPPLY ASSOCIATION 
Pursuant to Rules 211 and 214 of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s 
(“Commission’s”) Rules of Practice and Procedure, 18 C.F.R. §§ 385.211 and 385.214, the 
Retail Energy Supply Association (“RESA”)1 hereby files this Motion to Intervene and Protest in 
the above-referenced proceeding, in which PJM Interconnection, LLC (“PJM”) seeks to modify 
the Reliability Assurance Agreement (“RAA”) of its Open Access Transmission Tariff (“Tariff”) 
to establish a Reliability Backstop Procurement (“RBP”) process to procure new capacity to 
address resource adequacy issues in PJM (“RBP Proposal”).     
RESA files this Protest to express the need for market certainty, stability and clarity and 
the importance of the granular allocation of costs using principles of cost causation.   As 
described below, significant changes to the PJM market design can cause harm if implemented to 
upset settled expectations of Market Participants and if a change in market design creates rate 
shock. In addition, RESA opposes PJM’s default methodology that would allocate costs 
1
The comments expressed in this filing represent the position of the Retail Energy Supply Association 
(RESA) as an organization but may not represent the views of any particular member of the Association.  Founded 
in 1990, RESA is a broad and diverse group of more than twenty retail energy suppliers dedicated to promoting 
efficient, sustainable and customer-oriented competitive retail energy markets.  RESA members operate throughout 
the United States delivering value-added electricity and natural gas service at retail to residential, commercial and 
industrial energy customers.  More information on RESA can be found at www.resausa.org.

2 
4900-3540-9097.1 
associated with the capacity procurement in accordance with RAA Schedule 8.  In support of this 
Motion to Intervene and Protest, RESA submits as follows: 
I. 
MOTION TO INTERVENE 
A. 
Correspondence and Communications 
Correspondence and communications regarding this matter should be addressed to the  
following person(s), and the same should also be designated for service on the Commission’s  
official list for this proceeding: 
Elizabeth W. Whittle  
Charles Iannello 
Nixon Peabody LLP 
Interstate Gas Supply, LLC 
799 Ninth Street, N.W. 
6100 Emerald Parkway 
Suite 500 
Dublin, OH 43016 
 
Washington, DC 20001 
217-899-2537 
202-585-8338  
charlie.iannello@igs.com
ewhittle@nixonpeabody.com
B. 
RESA 
RESA is a non-profit trade association of independent corporations that are involved in the 
competitive supply of electricity and natural gas to end-use consumers.  RESA and its members 
are actively involved in retail electricity and natural gas markets throughout the United States in 
states that have implemented markets that allow entities other than the incumbent electric or natural 
gas utility to provide commodity electric and gas service. RESA members are Load Serving 
Entities (“LSEs”) active in the following RTO/ISOs: PJM, ISO New England, Inc. (“ISO-NE”), 
Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc. (“MISO”), New York Independent System 
Operator, Inc. (“NYISO”), and California Independent System Operator, Inc. (“CAISO”).  RESA 
members possess market-based rate authority from the Commission.

3 
4900-3540-9097.1 
C. 
Motion to Intervene  
On July 31, 2026, PJM made a filing to modify the RAA provisions of its Tariff to impose 
an RBP on a one-time basis to acquire additional capacity due to shortages for 2027/2028 and 
2028/2029 Reliability Pricing Model Auctions.  RESA, with members who are active in PJM 
markets, have an interest in this proceeding that cannot be represented by any other party, moves 
to intervene. 
II. 
GENERAL COMMENTS 
 RESA asks that the Commission take note of the need for market certainty and stability 
and the importance of granular cost allocations consistent with cost causation principles.2  In light 
of today’s ever increasing capacity prices, rate shock caused by mis-allocated costs will cause 
significant harm to those entities who are not causing the costs to increase.   
RESA members purchase services in the RTO/ISO markets such as energy, capacity and 
ancillary services, but they offer more than just electricity service to their customers.  Competitive 
retail suppliers may provide  retail energy to end-use customers at contracted fixed or variable 
prices which are tied to wholesale electricity prices.  Retail suppliers may offer demand response 
services – assisting customers in reducing peak demand and receiving benefits for reducing 
consumption at peak times.  Retail suppliers may offer energy efficiency services to assist 
customers in reducing their electricity consumption.  Retail suppliers may offer electricity with a 
certain component of renewable energy – or all renewable energy.  There is no one model – 
2  
Cost causation requires “all approved rates reflect to some degree the costs actually caused by the customer 
who must pay them.”  K N Energy v FERC, 968 F.2d 1295, 1300 (D.C. Cir. 1992); Midwest ISO Transmission 
Owners v FERC, 373 F.3d 1361, 1368 (D.C. Cir. 2004).

4 
4900-3540-9097.1 
competitive wholesale markets and the introduction of retail choice in states such as Ohio, Illinois, 
Pennsylvania, New Jersey, Delaware and Maryland, have allowed significant innovation, which 
has reduced consumption of energy, lowered prices, and provided valuable services to consumers.   
Competitive retail suppliers operate in an environment of risk.  Retail suppliers are unlike 
traditional utilities in several important ways.  For example, retail suppliers are not cost-based 
regulated by state public utility commissions (although they comply with a myriad of state 
requirements to be authorized to provide energy-related products and services to retail customers).  
Retail suppliers do not have a mechanism to defer costs, like traditional utilities, and thus bear the 
risk of wholesale market volatility and uncertainty.  Retail suppliers do not have a specified service 
area.  They contract with customers bilaterally.  Generally, these contracts are long-term – of a 
duration of one to five years. As a result, when a contract expires, it may or may not be renewed.  
Thus, a customer today may not be a customer tomorrow.  As a result, charges allocated to a utility 
service area or load zone must be properly allocated to the appropriate retail end use customer, 
even if the customer has changed suppliers or returned to default service (i.e. the customer is served 
by different LSEs).   
To offer valuable and innovative services at competitive prices, retail suppliers 
participating in competitive wholesale markets require market certainty, transparency and stability.  
Market certainty, transparency and stability allow retail suppliers to offer products and services 
that they know they can deliver during the term of the applicable contract.  The importance of 
having confidence in the competitive wholesale market cannot be overstated.  As with products 
and services offered by retail suppliers, the contracts vary by company, by service, by customer 
type, by term and other conditions.  If competitive retail suppliers are participating in default 
service programs, those programs often require winning suppliers to agree to a standard form

5 
4900-3540-9097.1 
contract, which may or may not address unanticipated market changes, including changes to 
capacity cost allocations caused by RBP.   
This RBP filing, and the related Interim Resource Adequacy Service (“IRAS”), filed by 
PJM in Docket No. ER26-3515, may fundamentally alter the risks and credit exposure of all 
customers in a utility service area depending on how RBP or related costs are allocated among 
them.  It is critical for all Market Participants to have market certainty, stability and transparency 
in this critical time as PJM addresses the need for additional capacity.  
 III. 
PROTEST 
A. The Commission should Deny PJM’s Default Allocation Proposal and Require 
PJM to Use Sub-Accounts to Allocate Costs to Large Load  
RESA supports PJM's RBP Proposal to the extent that it assigns RBP costs and collateral 
obligations to the LSE serving the Large Load Customers that cause those costs. PJM’s proposal 
to facilitate the allocation of costs to cost causers, however, is undermined to the extent that PJM’s 
proposed default methodology applies. Under PJM’s RBP, if an Electric Distributor does not report 
Reliability Backstop Obligations (“RBO”) for the Large Load Customers in its zone, PJM will 
instead allocate RBP costs to all load in that zone based on each LSE’s existing Peak Load 
Contribution assignments.  The result is that the cost of capacity procured specifically to serve 
new, not-yet-interconnected Large Load through the RBP would be borne by residential, 
commercial, and traditional industrial customers who did not cause those costs and who receive 
no corresponding benefit.  
This is not a remote contingency.  As PJM acknowledges, neither the Commission nor PJM 
can dictate how RBP costs are allocated among the customers and LSEs behind each Electric 
Distributor. Ensuring allocation of RBP costs to cost causers will require each Relevant Electric

6 
4900-3540-9097.1 
Retail Regulatory Authority (“RERRA”) and each Electric Distributor across the PJM footprint to 
implement regulations, tariff provisions, registry processes, and data exchanges necessary to 
identify Large Load Customers and assign RBO to their LSEs. Changes necessary to implement 
RBO may even require a change in state law or be dependent on PJM implementing the necessary 
changes to implement RBO.  While the commitments made today will not be paid until the 
2028/2029 Delivery Year, this is a significantly compressed schedule for the States and RERRAs 
to execute the necessary changes to implement RBO.  If the necessary changes are not 
implemented in time, the default allocation attaches automatically, and capacity costs associated 
with Large Load Customers are spread across non-cost causing residential, commercial and 
traditional industrial customers. In other words, the most consequential cost allocation outcome in 
this proceeding would be determined not by a reasoned Commission judgment about cost 
causation, but by the pace of administrative implementation in individual states, RERRAs and 
Electric Distributor service territories. 
PJM touts its cost allocation proposal as supporting the Statement of Principles Regarding 
PJM issued on January 16, 2026, by the National Energy Dominance Council and the 13 governors 
of the PJM states (“NEDC/PJM Governors’ Principles”)3
Thus, a cost allocation methodology that provides PJM states and/or RERRAs with the 
ability to determine the specific RBOs that should be assigned to LSEs, as well as to cost 
allocate to end-use customers in their respective states in accordance with their laws and 
policies, supports the NEDC/PJM Governors’ Principles, which include the principle that 
the cost of new capacity should be allocated to data centers who have caused the need for 
additional capacity in the PJM Region.4
3 Statement of Principles Regarding PJM, National Energy Dominance Council, 1 (Jan. 16, 2026), 
https://www.energy.gov/documents/statement-principles-regarding-pjm 
4 PJM RBP Proposal Filing Letter at 106-107.

7 
4900-3540-9097.1 
However, if for any reason, the states, RERRAs, and Electric Distributors are unable to 
timely implement the necessary changes to implement RBO, the NEDC/PJM Governor’ Principles 
would be gravely violated by the socialization of RBP costs against all captive customers.  There 
is a mechanism to prevent any unjustified cost allocations to LSEs – PJM should establish as a 
default methodology the obligation to create a sub-account to the LSE serving the Large Load 
where those costs can be appropriately assigned.  For these reasons, RESA respectfully requests 
the Commission reject PJM’s default zonal cost allocation proposal and require PJM to establish 
an LSE sub-account associated with the Large Load in the PJM system where the costs can be 
directly assigned.   
B.
If the Commission Accepts PJM’s Default Allocation Proposal, PJM Should be 
Ordered to Take Additional Steps to Protect Residential, Commercial and 
Traditional Industrial Customers from Cost Shifts  
If the Commission accepts PJM’s Tariff proposal to, as a default, allocate RBP costs to 
LSEs based on the sum of their customers’ Peak Load Contributions, states, RERRAs and Electric 
Distributors will be under significant pressure to timely implement RBO.   Accordingly, RESA 
respectfully requests that the Commission facilitate discussions among and between the states, 
RERRAs, Electric Distributors and interested Market Participants to assist in implementing the 
RBP Proposal and RBO.   
RESA hereby emphasizes the urgency of state action and collaboration between the states 
and PJM in implementing RBO. If the RBP Proposal is accepted substantially as filed, every PJM 
state — and particularly those open to retail competition — will need to move immediately to 
identify Large Load Customers and to assign RBP costs and collateral obligations to those 
customers and their LSEs.  RESA intends to participate in those proceedings, and the Commission 
should recognize in any order approving the RBP that the reasonableness of the cost allocation

8 
4900-3540-9097.1 
outcome depends entirely on the implementation of the necessary changes by states, RERRAs and 
Electric Distributors to complete implementation of RBO before obligations attach to all LSEs 
serving load in a zone. 
If PJM’s default allocation proposal is accepted as filed, and the Commission declines to 
implement RESA’s suggestion to create an LSE sub-account for Large Load as noted in Section 
IV.A above, then the Commission should require PJM to take additional steps to protect customers 
and LSEs before the default RPB cost allocation is triggered.  First, PJM should be required to 
publish, well in advance of each cost allocation determination, which zones lack a qualifying 
framework for identifying Large Load Customers and assigning Reliability Backstop Obligations.  
States, RERRAs, LSEs, and customers need notice of that exposure before the RBP costs are 
allocated, not after. Second, if the Commission nonetheless permits a default allocation, the Tariff 
should make clear that it is a last resort of strictly limited duration and that it establishes no 
precedent for allocating costs caused by Large Load to customers other than Large Load. 
C. 
The Commission Should Require Certain Commitments and Advance 
Disclosure from PJM to Reduce Risk and Provide Greater Certainty to 
LSEs.   
PJM’s RBP injects significant uncertainty to competitive wholesale markets to the 
detriment of wholesale and retail customers. In the short amount of time to analyze this filing, 
RESA has identified a number of concerns that are identified below. 
First, PJM should publish RBO determinations and resulting cost allocations expeditiously.  
Retail suppliers such as RESA members are currently submitting bids into default service supply 
solicitations to provide service to retail customers for long-term obligations of between one and 
five years.  Price certainty and the RBO is critical information in responding to these procurements

9 
4900-3540-9097.1 
for future Delivery Years.  The central RBP auction is proposed to run from September 30 through 
October 21, 2026, while the facilitated bilateral matchmaking process is expected to continue for 
another six to nine months.  Thus, RESA asks that the Commission require PJM to publish 
Reliability Backstop Obligation determinations and cost allocations sufficiently in advance of 
those solicitations for suppliers to reflect them in their offers.   
Second, PJM offers no guarantee regarding timing of resettlement of RBP charges.  RESA 
asks the Commission to confirm that RBP charges will not be subject to retroactive resettlement 
outside PJM's standard resettlement window. Retail suppliers cannot recover charges retroactively 
imposed after a contract has been priced and served, and the magnitude of the obligations at issue 
here makes that exposure materially different from ordinary settlement variance. 
Third, RESA further notes that excluding Large Load growth from future Reliability 
Pricing Model auction demand until that load is covered by new supply is directionally consistent 
with cost causation and may reduce capacity costs for all LSEs and the customers they serve. To 
realize that benefit, however, RESA asks that PJM be directed to re-release the 2029/2030 Base 
Residual Auction planning parameters promptly upon any change to the load forecast so suppliers 
can reflect a demand adjustment of this significance in their estimate of future capacity costs 
procured through the RPM. 
Fourth, PJM’s proposal appears to lack specificity around how RBP costs will be assigned 
to LSE’s serving Large Load Customers as those customers switch from one LSE to another 
throughout the period the RBP will be in effect.  For example, each state that permits retail access 
has rules and guidelines governing switching LSEs.  Under the RBP, how will PJM be notified of 
the transfer of the Large Load and how will appropriate collateral be collected from the transferee 
LSE and returned to the transfer LSE?  Will PJM deadlines interfere with the switch and leave the

10 
4900-3540-9097.1 
transfer LSE with the Large Load?  These issues must be addressed in the PJM Tariff. 
Finally, while PJM’s proposal provides detailed steps to address LSE default on RBP 
obligations, the proposal lacks details related to Large Load Customer load not materializing or 
decommissioning.  RESA supports the portion of the proposal intended to protect traditional 
customers if a Large Load Customer ceases operations after its load clears the RBP and requests 
that the Commission require PJM to address that scenario more completely.  For example, PJM’s 
proposal does not resolve whether the remaining fifteen-year cost obligation would be socialized 
to other customers in the zone, satisfied by drawing on an LSE's collateral, or reallocated. That 
ambiguity exposes non-cost causing customers and their LSEs to an open-ended liability and, as a 
practical matter, is itself an impediment to the Large Load interconnection the RBP is intended to 
facilitate. 
WHEREFORE, RESA respectfully requests that RESA’s Motion to Intervene is granted 
and its Protest considered by the Commission in this proceeding.  
Respectfully submitted, 
Elizabeth W. Whittle 
Elizabeth W. Whittle 
Counsel for 
The Retail Energy Supply Association 
Of Counsel: 
Nixon Peabody, LLP 
799 9th Street, N.W. 
Suite 500 
Washington, DC 20001 
202-585-8338 
ewhittle@nixonpeabody.com
Dated: August 21, 2026

11 
4900-3540-9097.1 
CERTIFICATE OF SERVICE 
I hereby certify that I have this day served the foregoing document, via email, on each 
person listed on the Official Service List compiled by the Secretary in this proceeding. 
Dated in Washington, DC this 21st day of August 2026. 
Elizabeth W. Whittle
Elizabeth W. Whittle
